analysis.one_liner: Eliminates the federal tax on capital gains for individuals and estates.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have repealed the capital gains tax, was introduced with 8 cosponsors and died in committee without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Rep. Joe Knollenberg's bill would have removed capital gains — the profit from selling stocks, bonds, real estate, and other assets held more than a year — from taxable income entirely for everyone except corporations. Today those gains are taxed at preferential rates; this bill would have made them tax-free. It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Households with large investment portfolios. Capital gains are heavily concentrated at the top: most households realize little or no taxable capital gain in a given year, while the biggest gains flow to the wealthiest taxpayers. Eliminating the tax would primarily benefit those who live off asset sales, and it would reduce federal revenue, which must be made up through borrowing or other taxes.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wealthy households with large investment gains

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the tax code so that 'gross income shall not include an amount equal to the net capital gain of the taxpayer for the taxable year' for any taxpayer other than a corporation, making capital gains entirely tax-free. [S3]

It would take effect for tax years beginning after December 31, 1998, immediately repealing the existing preferential capital gains rates in section 1(h) and removing capital gains from the alternative minimum tax base. [S3]
The CRS summary confirms the bill excludes net capital gain from gross income for all taxpayers other than corporations. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers broadly. Capital gains taxes raise substantial revenue, and eliminating them would enlarge the deficit or force other taxes to rise. Because capital gains accrue overwhelmingly to high-income households, the bill's benefits would be concentrated at the top while the cost of filling the gap would be spread across everyone else.

drawbacks.text: The benefit is sharply tilted toward the wealthy: capital gains income is concentrated among high earners and large investors, so a full exemption delivers most of its value to households that already pay the highest rates on their ordinary income. [S3]
The bill provides no replacement revenue. Eliminating a major revenue source without offsets increases the deficit or shifts the tax burden to wages, which ordinary workers pay at full rates. [S3]
A zero rate on capital gains widens the gap between how work and wealth are taxed, creating an incentive to restructure income as asset gains rather than wages or salary. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits flow almost entirely to the households with the largest investment gains, while the cost — lost federal revenue — falls on the general taxpayer through deficits or higher other taxes. It contained no offsetting revenue provisions, no phase-outs for high earners, and no protections for the Treasury. Even supporters of lower capital gains taxes generally pursued partial rate cuts rather than full repeal; this bill went far beyond that without addressing the cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and sat there for the rest of the two-year Congress, never getting a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Knollenberg introduced the Job Creation Act of 1999 on January 6, 1999, the first day of the 106th Congress. [S5]
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which writes tax law, on January 6, 1999. [S5]
The sponsor delivered introductory remarks printed in the Congressional Record on January 7, 1999. [S5]
Eight representatives cosponsored the bill — 7 Republicans and 1 Democrat. [S4]
No further action was taken; the bill never left committee and received no vote in either chamber before the Congress ended on January 3, 2001. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained directly, since the bill never became law. The outcome left in place the existing preferential capital gains rates and the federal revenue they raise, sparing other taxpayers from covering the cost of a full repeal that would have primarily benefited the wealthiest investors.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Other taxpayers, since the repeal never advanced

for.name: Rep. Joe Knollenberg
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the 106th Congress and delivered introductory remarks. [S5]

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on January 6, 1999 and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress — no hearing, no markup, no vote. [S5]

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken. The bill's sponsor and 7 of its 8 cosponsors were Republicans, with 1 Democratic cosponsor, but the committee took no action, so no chamber-wide position was ever recorded. [S4]

industries.note: The bill would have made capital gains — income concentrated among the top-earning households — entirely tax-free, while the lost revenue would be borne by other taxpayers or the deficit. [S3]

industries.industry: Financial services and asset markets (brokerages, funds, exchanges)
industries.note: A zero capital gains rate would encourage more asset selling and investment activity, benefiting firms that earn fees on trades and fund management. Any boost to investment would be paired with a large revenue loss falling on the general taxpayer. [S3]
